records.title: Overhaul data model of dependency graphs for better query performance and relationship type support
records.body:
### Current Behavior ### How Dependency Graphs Work Today Both the `PROJECT` and `COMPONENT` object have a `DIRECT_DEPENDENCIES` column, which contains a JSON array of serialized [`ComponentIdentity`](https://github.com/DependencyTrack/dependency-track/blob/master/src/main/java/org/dependencytrack/model/ComponentIdentity.java) objects. This roughly resembles how dependencies are represented in CycloneDX v1.5 and earlier. While this approach works, it has a few downsides: * Referential integrity can't be verified by the RDBMS. Since IDs are encoded in JSON, foreign keys can't be utilized. * Poor query performance. Traversing the graph requires expensive `LIKE` conditions such as `"DIRECT_DEPENDENCIES" LIKE ('%' || :childComponentUuid || '%')`. * Per default, DT does not create a working index on the `DIRECT_DEPENDENCIES` column * A `LIKE` condition with wildcards on both ends requires a special index, such as [GIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.1/textsearch-indexes.html) in PostgreSQL, which in turn requires an extension that is not enabled per default. * It bloats table sizes and REST API responses, since JSON arrays can become quite large for projects with busy dependency graphs. To give an example of how traversal queries look like in the current data model, here's one [from Hyades](https://github.com/DependencyTrack/hyades-apiserver/blob/032a6eb0d59086bc3418d5ec7120c715c9408b20/src/main/java/org/dependencytrack/policy/cel/CelCommonPolicyLibrary.java#L417-L482) that identifies whether a specific component (identified by the parameter `:leadComponentUuid`) is introduced through another component with the name `foo`:
Example Query 
-- Determine the project the given leaf component is part of.
WITH RECURSIVE
"CTE_PROJECT" AS (
  SELECT
    "PROJECT_ID" AS "ID"
  FROM
    "COMPONENT"
  WHERE
    "UUID" = :leafComponentUuid
),
-- Identify the IDs of all components in the project that
-- match the desired criteria.
"CTE_MATCHES" AS (
  SELECT
    "ID"
  FROM
    "COMPONENT"
  WHERE
    "PROJECT_ID" = (SELECT "ID" FROM "CTE_PROJECT")
    -- Do not consider other leaf nodes (typically the majority of components).
    -- Because we're looking for parent nodes, they MUST have direct dependencies defined.
    AND "DIRECT_DEPENDENCIES" IS NOT NULL
    AND ("NAME" = 'foo') -- NB: These could be arbitrarily many conditions
),
"CTE_DEPENDENCIES" ("UUID", "PROJECT_ID", "FOUND", "PATH") AS (
  SELECT
    "C"."UUID"                                       AS "UUID",
    "C"."PROJECT_ID"                                 AS "PROJECT_ID",
    ("C"."ID" = ANY(SELECT "ID" FROM "CTE_MATCHES")) AS "FOUND",
    ARRAY ["C"."ID"]::BIGINT[]                       AS "PATH"
  FROM
    "COMPONENT" AS "C"
  WHERE
    -- Short-circuit the recursive query if we don't have any matches at all.
    EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM "CTE_MATCHES")
    -- Otherwise, find components of which the given leaf component is a direct dependency.
    AND "C"."DIRECT_DEPENDENCIES" LIKE ('%' || :leafComponentUuid || '%')
  UNION ALL
  SELECT
    "C"."UUID"                                       AS "UUID",
    "C"."PROJECT_ID"                                 AS "PROJECT_ID",
    ("C"."ID" = ANY(SELECT "ID" FROM "CTE_MATCHES")) AS "FOUND",
    ARRAY_APPEND("PREVIOUS"."PATH", "C"."ID")        AS "PATH"
  FROM
    "COMPONENT" AS "C"
  INNER JOIN
    "CTE_DEPENDENCIES" AS "PREVIOUS" ON "PREVIOUS"."PROJECT_ID" = "C"."PROJECT_ID"
  WHERE
    -- If the previous row was a match already, we're done.
    NOT "PREVIOUS"."FOUND"
    -- Also, ensure we haven't seen this component before, to prevent cycles.
    AND NOT ("C"."ID" = ANY("PREVIOUS"."PATH"))
    -- Otherwise, the previous component must appear in the current direct dependencies.
    AND "C"."DIRECT_DEPENDENCIES" LIKE ('%' || "PREVIOUS"."UUID" || '%')
)
SELECT BOOL_OR("FOUND") FROM "CTE_DEPENDENCIES";
### CycloneDX v1.6 CycloneDX v1.6 will introduce the `provides` attribute to its `Dependency` model ([source](https://github.com/CycloneDX/specification/pull/366)): ```proto message Dependency { // References a component or service by the its bom-ref attribute string ref = 1; // The bom-ref identifiers of the components or services that are dependencies of this dependency object. repeated Dependency dependencies = 2; // The bom-ref identifiers of the components or services that define a given specification or standard, which are provided or implemented by this dependency object. repeated string provides = 3; } ``` In order to support this, and potential future additions to relationships, we need to rework how we handle dependency graphs. ### Proposed Behavior I propose to revisit how we store and traverse dependency graphs. Ideally, the graph structure would live in separate tables, and would be able to refer to multiple object types, such as

records.title: feat(compiler-world): build phase-labelled module graph and deterministic SCC schedule
records.body:
Parent: #2425 / #2559
Depends on module inputs: #2493
Accepted workspace capture: #8642
Static module resolution: #2468
Canonical environment/include roots: #7419, #7420, #7421
Fact producers: #4746, #4810
Consumers: next compiler-world snapshot PR, #5241, #4241, #5216

## One-PR outcome

Build a deterministic phase-labelled module dependency graph and SCC-condensed schedule from one accepted workspace generation and validated #2493 `CompileModule` inputs. This PR does not apply compile effects, publish a compiler-world snapshot, invalidate providers, or change live LSP behavior.

## Problem

Per-file module requests and imports do not establish cross-file compiler semantics until they share canonical module/source identity, phase labels, explicit unresolved/dynamic boundaries, and a deterministic cycle schedule. A simple package-name graph or filesystem adjacency would conflate compile-time `use`, runtime `require`, inheritance/composition, imports, generated relations, and unknown dynamic edges.

## Objective

Define one versioned graph equivalent to:

```text
CompilerModuleGraph
  accepted workspace/project generation identity
  module nodes from validated #2493 inputs
  phase-labelled typed edges
  unresolved/dynamic edge records
  deterministic SCC membership
  condensed DAG and stable schedule
  provenance/completeness/limitations
  graph fingerprint and validation receipt
```

## Edge contract

Represent edge dimensions separately rather than one overloaded enum. Preserve at least:

```text
relation kind
  use / require / import / export / parent / base / role-or-composition /
  generated / framework / other governed relation

phase
  compile / unitcheck-check-init / runtime / unknown-or-dynamic

resolution
  exact module/source target
  finite candidates
  unresolved
  external unavailable
  dynamic boundary

source evidence
  owning module/fact/effect/request ID
  exact anchor where source-backed
  producer/provenance/confidence/completeness
  source tier and limitations
```

Exact vocabulary may follow existing contracts. Do not flatten relation, phase, resolution, and proof into a single display string.

## Graph construction

- Capture one accepted #8642 workspace/project generation.
- Validate every #2493 module input belongs to that generation/root/configuration/environment.
- Consume exact #2468 resolutions where available; retain unresolved/dynamic requests as typed graph limitations rather than guessing edges.
- Keep compile-time and runtime-only edges distinct.
- Preserve inheritance/composition and import/export relationships without treating all as compile scheduling edges.
- Isolate same-name modules across roots and source tiers.
- Define deterministic duplicate/conflict policy by canonical edge identity.
- Build forward and reverse adjacency for the graph object; reverse invalidation policy remains a later PR.

## SCC and scheduling

- Compute strongly connected components over the exact edge classes admitted to the selected compile schedule.
- Give SCCs stable deterministic identities derived from normalized member/edge identities, not traversal order.
- Produce a deterministic condensed DAG and schedule.
- Preserve internal SCC edge/order evidence and explicit cycle limitations.
- Unknown/dynamic edges cannot be silently omitted while the graph claims globally complete scheduling; return typed bounded/partial schedule state.
- Adding a runtime-only edge must not perturb the compile schedule unless the declared profile says it is compile-relevant.

## Validation

Reject:

- dangling module/edge endpoints;
- cross-root identity leakage;
- mixed workspace/configuration/environment generations;
- exact edge without exact target authority;
- duplicate conflicting edge semantics;
- unstable SCC identity/order;
- schedule that violates condensed-DAG dependencies;
- cycle membership inconsistent with graph edges;
- graph completeness stronger than unresolved/dynamic inputs permit.

Emit stable typed codes and a deterministic graph/schedule receipt.

## Fixtures

- A → B → C acyclic compile graph;
- A ↔ B cycle plus downstream C;
- several independent SCCs with deterministic order;
- compile-time `use` versus runtime `require`;
- parent/base/import/export relations;
- finite candidate, unresolved, dynamic, and external dependency edges;
- same module name in two roots;
- workspace plus exact read-only dependency module;
- generated/framework relation with and without source anchor;
- add/remove/rename edge and module;
- insertion-order, host-path, Unicode, and newline determinism.

## Negative controls

Fail when graph construction rescans source, identifies modules by package/path text alone, treats runtime `require` as compile schedule by default, drops unresolved edges while claiming complete, lets map/Tarjan traversal order change SCC IDs or schedule, merges roots, invents source targets, or mutates the accepted workspace snapshot.

## Acceptance

- [ ] One versioned phase-labelled compi

records.title: Repair GLB/glTF imports and add safe imported-asset deletion
records.body:
## Observed defects

The current v0.9 Windows build can preserve enough hierarchy to keep a complex vehicle mostly assembled, but the imported result is still not production-correct.

Observed in the Maruti Suzuki Alto import:

- Several mesh/material entries report `Maximum call stack size exceeded`.
- Canonical conversion appears to recurse unsafely through some node/material data.
- Material fidelity is incomplete and the model is displayed with a mostly uniform fallback tint.
- Grounding/placement uses the aggregate bounds in a way that leaves wheels/body intersecting terrain.
- The large aggregate selection bounds are difficult to inspect.
- Imported assets cannot be safely deleted from the asset library.
- The UI needs a cleaner import state and repair flow.

## Required importer repairs

- Validate scene/node indices before traversal.
- Detect cycles and repeated references.
- Replace unsafe recursive traversal with iterative traversal or strict visited/depth guards.
- Preserve multiple scene roots and repeated mesh instances.
- Apply full node world transforms.
- Apply inverse-transpose normal transforms.
- Correct mirrored winding.
- Validate accessors, buffer views, byte ranges, component types, strides, and primitive modes.
- Preserve and report materials, texture slots, samplers, alpha modes, double-sided state, skins, animations, morph targets, and unsupported extensions.
- Isolate failure to the offending primitive/node rather than failing the whole import.
- Produce clear health-report diagnostics with node/mesh/material identifiers.
- Rebuild canonical derivatives without overwriting the source.
- Add asset-specific placement grounding using support/contact points rather than only aggregate AABB minimum.

## Safe deletion requirements

- Add `Archive`, `Delete import`, and `Restore` actions.
- Inspect scene usages and dependencies before deletion.
- Block destructive deletion while a scene still references the asset unless the user explicitly removes/replaces those usages.
- Remove or archive canonical derivatives, repair derivatives, LODs, collision, thumbnails, previews, Asset Recipes, Surface Recipe links, marketplace/job links, and staged files.
- Update the asset graph and scene usage indexes atomically.
- Keep an audit record and support undo/restore where practical.
- Never delete outside managed project directories.
- Report leftover/orphan references instead of hiding them.

## UI cleanup

- Separate import status, warnings, repairs, usages, provenance, and destructive actions.
- Show `Imported`, `Processing`, `Needs repair`, `Failed`, `Draft`, `Approved`, and `Archived` states clearly.
- Put destructive actions in a dedicated danger area with confirmation.
- Add `Remove preview` and `Cancel placement` behavior that cannot leave scene entities behind.

## Acceptance workflow

1. Import a simple GLB fixture.
2. Import a complex hierarchical vehicle GLB.
3. Confirm there is no stack overflow.
4. Confirm mesh parts stay assembled.
5. Confirm supported materials and textures are mapped correctly.
6. Confirm unsupported features are reported precisely.
7. Preview and ground the vehicle without wheels/body intersecting terrain.
8. Save, reload, and restart OmniForge.
9. Query scene usages.
10. Archive the import and restore it.
11. Attempt deletion while referenced and confirm it is blocked.
12. Remove the scene usage, delete the import, and confirm all managed derivatives are reconciled.
13. Undo/restore where supported.
14. Run full v0.5-v0.9 regression tests.

records.title: feat(reasoningbank): Entity graph for relationship tracking (gated on pipeline results)
records.body:
## Summary

Implement an entity graph to track relationships between entities mentioned in memories, enabling multi-hop reasoning and relationship queries. **This is the original #131 scope, preserved and gated on results from pipeline optimization issues A-D.**

**Parent Issue**: #123 (LoCoMo Benchmark Performance)
**Priority**: P2 — only implement if simpler optimizations fail to reach targets
**Previous Issue**: #131 (closed as not_planned, scope preserved here)

## ⚠️ Gating Condition

```
IF multi_hop_f1 < 35% AFTER implementing:
  - Issue A: Evaluation alignment (J-score)
  - Issue B: Memory granularity (session-level)
  - Issue C: Iterative search in harness
  - Issue D: Temporal reference resolution
THEN:
  Implement entity graph
ELSE:
  Close as "won't implement" — simpler solutions sufficed
```

## Background

Current search is query-to-document matching. This fails for questions requiring relationship traversal:

```
Q: Would Caroline still want to pursue counseling if she hadn't
   received support growing up?
```

This requires:
1. Find Caroline's career interest (counseling)
2. Find why she wants counseling (inspired by support she received)
3. Reason about counterfactual (no support → no inspiration → different career?)

## Design

Full design specification is preserved from #131 including:

- Entity and Relationship schema with alias support
- Graph interface (`EntityGraph`) with traversal operations
- SQLite-backed implementation (recommended for MVP)
- Entity extraction integration with fact extraction (#130)
- Search integration (entity-based boosting)
- Entity resolution with coreference handling

See #131 for the complete technical design.

## Implementation Tasks

- [ ] **Gate check**: Verify Issues A-D results don't meet targets
- [ ] Define entity and relationship schemas with alias support
- [ ] Create `internal/entitygraph/interface.go`
- [ ] Implement SQLite-backed graph store (separate DB per project)
- [ ] Add entity extraction from facts with coreference resolution
- [ ] Implement graph traversal (BFS path finding, max depth 2-3)
- [ ] Integrate graph with search (entity-based boosting)
- [ ] Add cleanup triggers for memory deletion
- [ ] Add MCP tools for graph queries
- [ ] Benchmark on LoCoMo multi-hop questions
- [ ] Document graph schema and query patterns

## Success Criteria

| Metric | Current | Target |
|--------|---------|--------|
| Multi-hop F1 | 8.85% | 40%+ |
| Multi-hop accuracy | 1/13 | 5/13+ |
| Relationship queries | N/A | Supported |

## References

- Original issue: #131 (closed, full technical design preserved)
- Fact extraction: #130
- Iterative search: #128 / #133
- Parent epic: #123

records.title: [Inductor] User-defined Triton access analysis is exponential on shared TTIR DAGs
records.body:
### Bug description

`torch._higher_order_ops.triton_kernel_wrap.analyze_kernel_access::_find_arg_access_count` traverses the user-defined Triton TTIR dataflow graph without memoizing `Intermediate` results. A shared subgraph is therefore re-expanded once per path reaching it. Repeated diamond/branch joins make one access analysis exponential in sharing depth.

This can make `torch.compile` appear to hang during Inductor lowering. In a real 24-argument user-defined Triton kernel, one call remained in this loop for 59 minutes before termination.

Strictly, for finite acyclic TTIR this is pathological algorithmic blow-up rather than an infinite loop. The observed run was practical nontermination:

- `py-spy --locals` placed the active main thread in `_find_arg_access_count`; the hottest child frame was the dataclass-generated `Intermediate.__hash__`, from repeated dictionary probes.
- The process held 100% of one CPU core with the GIL; only the main thread was active.
- GPU SM utilization stayed at 1-3% for 12 consecutive samples.
- Voluntary context switches changed by 2 in 5 seconds, excluding I/O, lock, and CUDA-sync waits.
- Inductor emitted no new compile artifacts for 15 minutes.

Current `main` still has the unbounded DFS:

```python
while stack:
    arg = stack.pop()
    ...
    elif isinstance(arg, Intermediate) and not arg.fake():
        for op in ops[arg]:
            ...
            stack.extend(op.args)
```

The issue originated when the former boolean reachability traversal with a `visited` set was replaced by access-path counting for user-kernel epilogue fusion in #173662. `_decide_can_fuse_epilogue` now requires `write_count[written_arg_index] == 1`.

### Minimal internal-IR reproducer

This constructs repeated shared branch joins directly in the analysis IR. Each added level approximately doubles work. Use a modest `DEPTH` first.

```python
from collections import defaultdict

from torch._higher_order_ops.triton_kernel_wrap import (
    Intermediate,
    Op,
    Param,
    analyze_kernel_access,
)

DEPTH = 24
ops = defaultdict(list)

prev = Intermediate(0)
ops[prev].append(Op("arith.extsi", None, [Param(0)], prev))

for i in range(1, DEPTH + 1):
    cur = Intermediate(i)
    # One producer consumes the same shared predecessor along two paths,
    # modeling repeated branch joins in TTIR.
    ops[cur].append(Op("arith.select", None, [Param(1), prev, prev], cur))
    prev = cur

sink = Intermediate(DEPTH + 1)
ops[sink].append(Op("tt.store", None, [prev, Param(2)], sink))
functions = {"kernel": dict(ops)}

analyze_kernel_access.reset()
analyze_kernel_access(
    functions,
    "kernel",
    1,
    ("out",),
    frozenset({0}),
)
```

The graph has O(`DEPTH`) nodes, but the loop performs O(2^`DEPTH`) expansions.

### Correctness constraint on the fix

A single global `visited` set is not a safe drop-in repair. Multiple write sinks may share an `Intermediate`; globally deduplicating the second path can change a genuine count from 2 to 1 and incorrectly enable epilogue fusion.

A semantics-preserving repair is to memoize, per `Intermediate` and `skip_loads` mode, a map from parameter index to downstream access multiplicity, then merge those summaries at joins. Since current consumers observe only:

- whether an argument appears in the map, and
- whether a write count is exactly 1,

counts can safely saturate at 2 (`0`, `1`, `many`). This avoids exponentially large integers as well as exponential traversal. Expected complexity is O((V + E) * P), where P is the number of kernel parameters represented in summaries. An in-progress marker should fail closed on an unexpected dataflow cycle.

### Relationship to #193227

#193227 is useful but orthogonal. It reduces repeated whole-kernel analyses across consumers and launch sites. It does not bound the first analysis of a new kernel signature, so a single shared TTIR DAG can still hit this blow-up before anything is cached.

### Environment

- PyTorch: `2.12.1+cu130`
- PyTorch git version: `7269437d655783a26cba32aa88195b741ff496aa`
- Triton: `3.7.1`
- Python: 3.12
- Reproduced in the user-defined Triton path reached from `torch.compile` / Inductor lowering

records.title: [BUG]: drizzle-kit generate/check is exponential in the number of merged migration branches
records.body:
### Report hasn't been filed before.

- [x] I have verified that the bug I'm about to report hasn't been filed before.

### What version of `drizzle-orm` are you using?

1.0.0-beta.21

### What version of `drizzle-kit` are you using?

1.0.0-beta.21 (also verified present in 1.0.0-beta.24, 1.0.0-rc.3, and 1.0.0-rc.4, the relevant code is unchanged across these releases)

### Other packages

_No response_

### Describe the Bug

#### Undesired behavior
Every drizzle-kit generate (and check) runs the commutativity detector
detectNonCommutative over the whole migration DAG. For each fork point it calls
collectLeaves, a DFS with no visited set, so it enumerates every root-to-leaf
path rather than every distinct leaf. When the migration history contains
merge “diamonds” (created whenever two migrations branch off a common parent and a
later snapshot lists both as parents) the number of paths is exponential in the
number of merges, and the detector runs a full-schema diff once per enumerated
path, all of them redundant.

```
collectLeaves(graph, startId) {
  const leaves = [];
  const stack = [startId];
  const prevToChildren = {};
  for (const node of Object.values(graph))
    for (const parentId of node.prevIds) (prevToChildren[parentId] ??= []).push(node.id);
  while (stack.length) {
    const id = stack.pop();
    const children = prevToChildren[id] ?? [];
    if (children.length === 0) leaves.push(id);
    else for (const child of children) stack.push(child); // ← no visited set
  }
  return leaves;
}
```

#### Environment
- Database engine: PostgreSQL
- Runtime: Bun
- dialect: "postgresql"


#### Steps to reproduce
Initialize a project and generate a baseline migration.
Build K stacked merge diamonds: from the current head, generate two migrations on
two branches off the same parent, then merge so drizzle-kit writes a snapshot whose
prevIds lists both leaf ids. Repeat K times.
Run drizzle-kit generate with no schema change and time it. Runtime grows ~2^K
(each added diamond roughly doubles it), even though it produces nothing.


#### Desired result
generate/check should be roughly linear in (migrations × snapshot size),
independent of how many branches have merged. Any one of these fixes would work I think:

1. Add a visited set to collectLeaves so it returns distinct leaves (O(V+E))
2. Deduplicate leaves before diffing (and/or memoize diffPostgres by
(parentId, leafId)), so a leaf reachable by multiple paths is diffed once.
3. Early-out detectNonCommutative when the global leaf count is ≤ 1 (linear or
fully merged history)


#### Workaround

I was able to work around this by cleaning up the snapshots prevId history to be linear, but of course just a temporary measure, so hoping for a long term fix so we don't need to rely on that.


Full disclosure: this is mostly my AI agent's diagnosis of the issue, it seems right to me but I wanted to open an issue rather put up a fix PR in case it doesn't seem right to you. Thanks!

# Content Notes
## Jaywalking
"Jaywalking" is named for avoiding cross tables, for express many-to-many relationship, and use list values instead. When trying to put multiple values in a single attribute, many problems occur: needing to use regular expression to match certain values (format may differ between SQL vendors), needing to JOIN tables to find related data, unable to use aggregation clauses, issuing multiple SQL for updating a specific data, and no validity on the value.

The solution is to create a cross table that holds foreign key between the two entities.
```mermaid

  ENTITY2 ||--o{ CROSS-TABLE : ""
```

> Store each value in a separate row and column.

## Naive Trees
Adding `parent_id` column to represent a tree structure data can be considered as "naive trees". This design is known as an "adjacency list", which is not the best choice for querying for all descendants as it requires JOIN-ing for each depth of the tree. Some database vendors support SQL extension for tree structured data, using `WITH` clause and Common Table Expression (CTE) to define recursive query.
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE Tree
  (id, parent_id, content)
AS (...)
```

Other alternative models that could be used to express tree structure data are: path enumeration model, nested set mode, and closure table model. Path enumeration resolves the efficiency of obtaining ancestor nodes, by storing the path like the UNIX file path. Nested set stores the set of descendants using two values `nsleft` and `nsright` (`nsleft` is given a value smaller than the value of every descendant node, `nsright` is given a value larger), which can be used to create queries for sub trees. Closure table stores not only the direct parent-child relationship, but the paths of the whole tree onto an independent table.

## ID Required
The primary key is a mechanism that guarantees the uniqueness of all rows in the table. Primary key can be in the form of natural key, pseudo or surrogate key, or compound key; therefore "id" of a table is not always required.

## Keyless Entry
In relational database architecture, it is important to design the relationship between tables, due to referential integrity reason. Use of foreign key prevents from mistakes from having partially updated data, and can use cascading updates that cannot be implemented in the application code.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Bugs (
  reported_by BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  ...
  FOREIGN KEY (reported_by) REFERENCES ...
    ON UPDATE CASCADE
    ON DELETE RESTRICT,  // -> restricts deletion of the referenced data
);
```

Despite foreign key constraints require some overhead, it is much more efficient than: eg. checking data (SELECT query) before some action, locking the table to make changes on multiple tables.

> To prevent mistakes on database, use foreign key constraints.

## Entity-Attribute-Value
When wanting to store variable attributes, the first solution that comes to mind is to store these values as records in a table. However this could lead to problems such as: not being able to find an expected attribute, attribute column cannot be constraint by data type as well as referential integrity.

There are 4 ways of avoiding this by using: single table inheritance, concrete table inheritance, class table inheritance, and  semi-structured data. Single table inheritance stores all attribute values as column, and when no attribute is given NULL is stored. Concrete table inheritance creates the table for each subtypes. Similarly, class table inheritance creates a parent table for common attributes, and for each other unique subtypes additional table is created. Lastly, semi-structured data is referred as storing data in XML or JSON format in a single cell.

## Polymorphic Associations
Polymorphic associations occur when storing foreign key manually by associating some data that is the id of a related table. The solution is to design a proper relation, eg. using cross tables.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Comments (
  comment_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  issue_id   BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL, // -> this id is used to reference multiple tables
  issue_type VARCHAR(20),              // -> issue_id is stored in either "Bugs" or "FeatureRequests"
  ...
);
```

> Relationship between tables always has only one source and one destination.

## Multicolumn Attributes
When storing attributes in multiple columns, this becomes an anti-pattern especially when the number of attributes is not known beforehand, eg. phone number of an address. It is recommended to create a dependent table, which the attributes will be easier to find, and guarantees uniqueness.

> Values with the same meaning should be stored in the same column.

## Scope

Portfolios can nest other portfolios (owner's aggregator case: one portfolio composing the Parqet-synced one + the BT-native one + its own rows).

- **Schema (append-only):** `portfolio_links` (parent_id, child_id, created_at; unique pair). Own portfolios only in v1 (shared-portfolio nesting = later, not now).
- **DAG rules (binding):** cycle detection at link insert (recursive CTE — inserting a link that creates any cycle is refused with a typed error), depth cap (env-tunable, default 3). **Aggregation flattens to a SET** — resolve the closure to unique portfolio ids, then compose; a portfolio reachable via two paths counts ONCE.
- **Composition semantics:** parent view = own rows + union of flattened children's rows, children **read-only in the parent** (edit at origin — PP1's rule, no rows copied, membership only). Value/series/stats compose by summing child series post-flatten with existing FX conversion; holdings merge per asset across children.
- **Exclusions:** encrypted portfolios can neither nest nor be nested (typed refusal). Nested children joining/leaving invalidates parent-derived caches.
- **UI:** Composition tab in portfolio settings (add/remove children, cycle/depth errors surfaced plainly), nested-row provenance chip ("from <portfolio>", click-through to origin), aggregate badges on the portfolio card. EN + DE.

## Acceptance

- Cycle + depth + double-count tests: D nests C and A, C nests A ⇒ A counted once everywhere (value, holdings, stats).
- Read-only enforcement: mutating a child's row via the parent context refuses; edit-at-origin works.
- Encrypted-portfolio exclusion enforced both directions.
- Full suite green; migration append-only; EN + DE complete.
